entries.meaning: “All the afflicted, sorrowing mothers will question me—what, Fate, shall I tell them? When Lakṣmaṇa’s mother asks, what comforting message can I give? Rāma’s mother will come running like a cow lowing as she remembers her calf; when she questions me, shall I answer only that Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Vaidehī have gone to the forest? Whoever asks, I must give that reply; this is the joy I go now to receive in Ayodhyā. And when the grief-stricken king, whose life depends upon Raghunātha, questions me, with what face can I say that I returned safely after delivering the princes? Hearing the message from Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sītā, the king will cast away his body like straw. My heart did not split like mud when separated from its beloved water; I know Fate gave me this body only as an instrument of torment.”

Lamenting along the road in this way, Sumantra’s chariot quickly reached the bank of the Tamasā. After respectfully dismissing the Niṣādas, who bowed at his feet and returned distraught with grief, he hesitated to enter the city like one guilty of killing guru, brahmin, and cow. Sitting beneath a tree, he let the day pass and waited for evening. In darkness he entered Ayodhyā, drew the chariot into the palace compound, and left it at the door. Everyone who heard the news came to the king’s gate to see it. Recognizing the chariot and seeing the horses distraught, their bodies dissolved as hail melts in sunlight. How anguished were the city’s women and men—like schools of fish as the water drains away. When news of the minister’s arrival reached the women’s quarters, everyone was overcome; the palace seemed terrible to him, like a dwelling of ghosts.

In extreme distress all the queens questioned Sumantra, but his faltering voice could form no answer. He could neither hear nor see clearly; whenever anyone asked, he only said, “Tell me—where is the king?” Seeing the minister deranged, the attendants led him to Kauśalyā’s chamber. There Sumantra saw the king like a moon bereft of nectar: without seat, bed, or ornaments, lying utterly soiled upon the ground. He sighed and brooded as if Yayāti had fallen from the gods’ city. Heaved by grief, his chest filled again and again, like Sampāti fallen with burnt wings. The king who loved Rāma repeated “Rāma, Rāma,” then “Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, Vaidehī.” Seeing him, Sumantra cried a blessing for long life and prostrated; hearing him, the distraught king rose and demanded, “Tell me, Sumantra—where is Rāma?”

The king drew Sumantra to his heart like a drowning man who had found some support. Seating him close with affection, the king asked through tear-filled eyes: “Tell me of Rāma’s welfare, loving friend. Where are Raghunātha, Lakṣmaṇa, and Vaidehī? Have you brought them back, or did they proceed into the forest?” Tears covered the minister’s eyes at the question. Grief-stricken, the king asked again for Sītā, Rāma, and Lakṣmaṇa’s message. Recalling Rāma’s form, virtues, character, and nature again and again, he tortured his heart. “I pronounced the forest exile; hearing it, my mind felt neither joy nor regret. Yet when separated from that son my life did not leave—what greater sinner can there be than me? Friend, take me wherever Rāma, Sītā, and Lakṣmaṇa are; otherwise, I tell you truly, my life now seeks to depart.”

Again and again the king asked the minister to tell his beloved son’s message and begged his friend quickly to devise some way to show Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sītā to his eyes. Sumantra gathered courage and spoke gently: “Great king, you are learned and wise, a brave, steadfast, foremost ruler; assemblies of holy people have always served you. Birth and death, every sorrow and experience, loss and gain, meeting and separation from those dear to us—all occur under the power of time and action, Lord, compulsively as night and day. The dull rejoice in happiness and wail in pain, while the steadfast hold both equal in the mind. Take courage through discriminating reflection and abandon grief, benefactor of all. Their first halt was on the Tamasā and the second beside the Gaṅgā; after bathing and drinking water, the two heroes remained there with Sītā.”

“The boatman rendered much service, and they spent that night at Śṛṅgaverapura. At dawn Rāma called for banyan milk and fashioned his own hair into a crown of matted locks. Rāma’s friend then summoned a boat. Raghurāya first helped his beloved aboard and followed; Lakṣmaṇa readied bow and arrows and boarded only upon the Lord’s command. Seeing me distraught, Raghubīra steadied himself and spoke sweetly: ‘Father, convey my reverence to father; again and again take hold of his lotus feet. Fall at his feet and petition him repeatedly not to be anxious about me. Through his grace, favor, and merit, our forest road is auspicious and all is well with us.’”

Rāma continued: “‘Look upon all the citizens and relatives and convey this petition of mine, father: in every way do whatever keeps the king content, for that is my true welfare. When Bharata returns, tell him not to abandon righteous statecraft after receiving the throne. Let him protect the subjects in deed, word, and thought and serve all the mothers, regarding them equally. Brother, fulfill a brother’s obligation by serving father, mothers, kinsmen, and attendants. Above all, keep the king in such a way that no one causes him anxiety on my account.’ Lakṣmaṇa spoke some harsh words, but Rāma restrained him and repeatedly charged me, upon his own oath, not to repeat Lakṣmaṇa’s youthful outburst. After offering reverence, Sītā tried to say something, but love made her faint; speech failed, her eyes filled with tears, and her thrilling body seemed to put forth new leaves.”

“At that moment Raghubara read my face, and the boatman rowed the boat to the far shore. The crest-jewel of Raghu’s line departed in this way while I stood and watched, holding my thunderbolt-hard chest. How can I tell my own anguish? I returned alive bearing Rāma’s message.” Saying this, the minister’s voice failed; loss, shame, and grief overwhelmed him. The moment the king heard his son’s words, he fell to the earth with a terrible burning in his breast. Thrashing in violent bewilderment, his mind was gripped like a fish assailed in the middle of a drying pool. All the queens wailed and wept; how can such great calamity be described? Hearing their lament, grief itself grieved and steadfastness itself lost courage. Ayodhyā filled with tremendous clamor at the sound of its king, like a vast flock of birds in a forest struck at night by a hard thunderbolt.

The king’s life rose into his throat; he writhed like a serpent deprived of its jewel. All his faculties became profoundly disturbed, like a lake of lotuses without water. Kauśalyā saw the king fading and knew inwardly that the sun of the solar line was setting. Rāma’s mother gathered courage and spoke as the moment required: “Lord, understand and reflect in your heart. Separation from Rāma is a boundless ocean; you are the helmsman of Ayodhyā’s ship, and the whole company of dear travelers has boarded it. If you retain courage, the far shore can be reached; otherwise the entire family will drown. Beloved, if you hold my plea in your heart, Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sītā will meet us again.” Hearing his beloved’s gentle words, the king opened his eyes and looked at her, like a gasping, sullied fish sprinkled with cool water.

Regaining some composure, the king sat up and asked Sumantra where compassionate Rāma was, where Lakṣmaṇa and Rāma’s loving companion were, and where his dear daughter-in-law Vaidehī was. Wailing in many ways, the distraught king endured a night that passed like an age. He remembered the blind ascetic’s curse and told Kauśalyā the whole former event. He became frantic as he narrated that history: “Shame upon the hope of life without Rāma. Why preserve the body that has not fulfilled my vow of love? Ah Raghunandana, dearer than life—without you I have lived far too many days! Ah Jānakī, ah Lakṣmaṇa, ah Raghubara; ah raincloud for the cātaka bird of your father’s heart!” Saying “Rāma” again and again, the king left his body in separation from Raghubara and went to the gods’ abode.
